analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and other countries.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to let Americans import cheaper prescription drugs never left the Senate health committee and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the federal government to write rules allowing prescription drugs to be imported into the United States. Individuals could bring in a personal supply, such as a three-month supply, and pharmacists and wholesalers could reimport drugs that were made in the U.S. and sold abroad for less. The bill was written to include safety safeguards and required a government study on the safety and trade effects of the imports.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs, especially seniors on Medicare and others on fixed incomes. The bill's own findings note that many people choose between buying medicine and paying for food or housing, and that the same U.S.-approved drugs sell for much less abroad [S3]. Pharmacists and drug wholesalers would also gain a new legal channel to buy lower-priced versions of U.S.-made drugs from other countries and pass the savings on [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying U.S. drug prices, especially seniors

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that drug costs are rising at an alarming rate and that millions of Americans, including Medicare beneficiaries on fixed incomes, face daily choices between medicine and necessities like food and housing [S3].

It would direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue regulations permitting importation of prescription drugs, letting individuals bring in a personal supply of up to about three months and letting licensed pharmacists and wholesalers reimport U.S.-made drugs sold at lower prices abroad [S3].

The bill includes safety requirements: importers must document the drug, the prescriber, and where and when it was purchased, and the regulations must provide reasonable assurance that imported products are safe and effective [S3].
It required a government study, reported to Congress within five years, evaluating the safety and purity of imported products and related patent and trade issues [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who currently sell the same medicines at substantially higher prices in the United States than abroad. The bill's own findings acknowledge that identical drugs 'are available in countries other than the United States at substantially lower prices' [S3]. Opening a legal import channel would expose U.S. prices to competition from those lower foreign prices.

drawbacks.text: Safety is the main objection. The bill's findings acknowledge that any import scheme 'should not endanger the gold standard for safety and effectiveness' maintained in the U.S., and the bill requires the Secretary to design additional safeguards based on the regulatory strength of the exporting country [S3]. Opponents have long argued that imported drugs are harder to track for counterfeiting, expiration, or improper handling.

The bill's benefit depends entirely on regulations the Secretary would have to write; it permits importation but does not itself guarantee it happens, and the compliance paperwork required of individuals and pharmacists could limit how much savings reach patients [S3].

The bill also required a study of 'other patent and trade issues' affecting safety or availability, an acknowledgment that importation raises intellectual-property and international-trade complications that could produce disputes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large and direct: cheaper access to medicines that people are already buying abroad or going without. The main cost is a genuine safety risk in monitoring a new import channel, which the bill tried to address through documentation requirements, pharmacist and wholesaler licensing limits, and a required study. The design is cautious rather than sweeping, but the outcome would depend heavily on how federal regulators wrote the rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 9, 2000 by Senator Jeffords, joined by Senators Wellstone, Snowe, and Collins [S3].
It had five cosponsors, split between two Democrats and three Republicans [S4].

It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, and the record shows no further action, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no passage before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers were better off: the bill died without a vote, so no lower-priced import channel was opened and U.S. drug prices remained the highest in the comparison group. Americans who might have bought cheaper imported medicines saw no change.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan: a Republican lead sponsor with two Democratic and three Republican cosponsors, and no vote was ever held, so no roll-call record shows how the parties split on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would open a legal channel for patients, pharmacists, and wholesalers to buy U.S.-approved drugs at the lower prices charged abroad, exposing U.S. prices to foreign competition. Because the bill died in committee, manufacturers kept their higher U.S. prices untouched.

The bill would have allowed licensed pharmacists and wholesalers to reimport U.S.-made drugs sold cheaper abroad, giving them a new supply channel they could pass savings through, subject to new documentation and tracking requirements. Their gain runs alongside patients' savings.
